articles.title: Fitch downgrades France's economic outlook from stable to negative
articles.text:
Fitch downgrades France's economic outlook from stable to negative
Advertisement
Politics
Fitch downgrades France's economic outlook from stable to negative
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 31 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 16:12 CET
Add a comment
The Eiffel Tower dominating the Paris skyline. Photo by Damien MEYER / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
The Fitch ratings agency on Friday maintained France's credit rating at A+ but downgraded its outlook from "stable" to "negative" as it raised new concerns over the cost of paying for the country's debt mountain.
The US agency predicted that the debt level for the European Union's second biggest economy would rise from nearly 115.7 percent of GDP in 2025 to 124 percent in 2028. Its last review in August had forecast that France's debt would reach 122.7 percent of GDP in 2028.
"Weaker growth, renewed fiscal deterioration and higher yields have increased the challenge of delivering the necessary sustained fiscal consolidation to arrest France's worsening debt trajectory," it said.
Advertisement
International investors have expressed widespread concern over France's debt level and this has pushed up the interest yields it pays to service debt, which is one of the highest in Europe.
The country will hold a two-round presidential election in April-May next year, and Fitch said the prospects for debt reduction after the vote were "uncertain".
It said the political divisions, with far-right and far-left candidates leading opinion poll surveys, would make it difficult to agree "a credible fiscal strategy".
"The emerging policy debate ahead of the presidential election has not materially strengthened Fitch's confidence in the prospects for durable deficit reduction that could lead to debt stabilization. Large protests over public services and living costs further complicate the social context for fiscal consolidation," it commented.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
The Fitch assessment came after the INSEE national statistics agency reported Friday that the economy has not grown so far this year and contracted in the period from July to September.
The government is also struggling to get parliament to pass its budget, aiming for a reduction in spending, for 2027. This has compounded market fears.
"If we fail to achieve the turnaround outlined in the budget, we are headed straight for a wall," Finance Minister Roland Lescure warned in a radio interview.

articles.title: Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
articles.text:
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
Presented by Talent Berlin
Why Berlin is still a magnet for international talent
There's far more to Berlin than its UNESCO-protected club culture. For those seeking an exciting career move, the German capital offers a heady mix of both business and pleasure.
Published: Thu 29 Oct 2026 15:45 CEST
Photo: Talent Berlin
For some, living and working abroad is a lifelong dream. It’s choosing where to start this new life that’s the million-dollar question. A city might offer great job opportunities but fall short on other things that make life outside work fulfilling—or vice versa.
In Berlin, you don't have to choose. As one of Europe's capitals for innovation and start-ups, it combines career opportunities with a rich cultural scene, more to do outside of work than one could manage in a lifetime, and a diverse international community ( around 25 per cent of Berliners are foreign-born).
It’s a city that’s famous for its tolerance and readiness to embrace different lifestyles. After all, Berliners aren't born—they're made at the Bürgeramt.
A city buzzing with ideas
Berlin's reputation as a start-up capital isn't just hype. In 2026, StartupBlink named it the EU's "Best Community-Driven Ecosystem". Its venture-backed start-ups are worth €169 billion and support some 94,000 jobs.
The Talent Berlin LinkedIn page posts Jobs of the Week, as well as other useful information about what's happening in Berlin's talent and innovation ecosystem.
Explore the Berlin-Brandenburg start-up ecosystem
While Berlin is home to one of Europe's leading start-up hubs, its business landscape is as varied as it is prolific. It has a booming tech sector, world-class life sciences and biotech communities, a growing green economy, and, famously, a thriving creative scene.
The city practically pulses with ideas and innovation; it's an incredibly exciting place to be for those working in science and research, biotechnology, and energy and environment, as well as other industries that will play a vital role in the decades to come.
Many of Berlin's innovations emerge where these industries intersect, from sustainable fashion and food science to digital health and the creative use of AI.
International professionals working in the city often cite its cross-sector ecosystem as one of its greatest advantages. Once you have your foot in the door, you can hop between start-ups, established companies, research, and emerging industries.
Photo: Talent Berlin
You won't get lost in translation
Learning a new language is all part of the fun of moving abroad, and German is, naturally, widely spoken in Berlin.
However, in those early days — or even years — of acclimatisation, you can easily get by in English, though it doesn't hurt to have a German-speaking friend who can help with certain administrative tasks.
Taking the time to learn German doesn't just expand your career options and make bureaucracy easier; it helps you integrate into Germany itself, not just Berlin's international community.
Keep up with Berlin’s start-up scene
If you’re serious about settling in Berlin for the long term, an integration or language course gives you essential German skills and practical knowledge of German society to help you live and work independently.
The city that never sleeps
In Berlin, when the 9-to-5 ends, the 5-to-9 begins.
Whatever you like to do in your spare time, whether you're into climbing, clubbing, or quite literally anything in between, you'll find it in Berlin.
The city’s tree-lined streets are crammed with cafes, bars, restaurants, and indie stores. Parks punctuate the city, and you're rarely more than a short journey from a wild swimming lake, forest, or nature reserve where you can enjoy the great outdoors.
Photo: Paula Schmidt / Pexels
Many Berliners forgo a car for a bike; the city is easy to cycle, and an extensive, affordable public transport system makes getting around without a car relatively straightforward.
The elephant in the room
Berlin is an attractive place to live, so its housing market is stretched—to put it lightly. That makes it tough to find somewhere to live, especially for newcomers.
Somewhat counterintuitively, you generally need to be in Berlin while searching for an apartment, so you can view the property and meet the landlord or estate agent before signing.
Many people start with temporary accommodation while they familiarise themselves with the rental process and look for a long-term contract.
Check with your employer about any relocation or housing assistance they may offer, and take a look at Talent Berlin's housing guide as a starting point. The organisation also offers a housing service your employer may already use, so it’s worth asking about this before you make the move.
Could Berlin be your next move?
Berlin has its quirks — some that make life easier, others that can make it more challenging. But for skilled professionals, few cities offer the same combination of career opportunity, innovation, internationalism, and life beyond work.
You may move to Berlin for the job, but it won't be the only reason you stay.

articles.title: Police fire tear gas as thousands march in France
articles.text:
Police fire tear gas as thousands march in France
Advertisement
Protests
Police fire tear gas as thousands march in France
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 31 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 17:16 CET
Add a comment
Protesters hold banners and flags during nationwide demonstrations over the rising cost of living and inequality organised by Yellow Vest movement, labour unions and high school and university students, in Marseille. Photo by Miguel MEDINA / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
French police fired tear gas and clashed with some protesters on Saturday as thousands marched across France against soaring living costs and police violence, with some demonstrators dressed as clowns and witches for Halloween.
While the third consecutive weekend of nationwide protests was largely peaceful, tensions erupted in several cities, including the southern port city of Marseille, where demonstrators clashed with police.
In Lyon, France's third-largest city, people threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire tear gas, according to a journalist at the scene.
In the southern city of Toulouse, police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators, some of them in costume.
READ ALSO: MAPS - Routes and Metro closures for the Paris demo on October 31st
In Paris, thousands of people, some wearing costumes ranging from Spider-Man to Frankenstein, walked through eastern Paris as a helicopter circled overhead.
Placards read: "No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak" and "Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween."
"We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students' demands, yes to giving citizens a voice," Camille Guerin, 31, said in the western city of Nantes.
Police said about 70,000 people demonstrated in Paris alone.
Officers had made 27 arrests by 2:00 pm on Saturday, compared with 217 arrests a week ago.
An aide to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that police had prepared for street violence on a scale "comparable" to the unrest two weeks ago, when shops were looted and public buildings set ablaze.
Between 400 and 800 hard-left activists were expected in Paris, said an informed source.
Advertisement
'Struggle is classy'
The demonstrations come in a febrile political climate, with presidential elections less than six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen topping opinion polls.
The protest movement, bringing together Yellow Vest activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on the rising cost of living, inequality, and deteriorating learning conditions.
Following a security clampdown and serious injuries to some protesters, the movement broadened its demands to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest.
Similar youth-led demonstrations have been seen across Europe in recent weeks.
Thousands of young Germans took to the streets nationwide on Saturday.
In the northern French city of Lille, 47-year-old Aurelie Herrmann danced at the protest.
"I dance because on television they only show damage and destruction, whereas you can perfectly well demonstrate in good spirits," she said.
"Struggle is classy, it needs to come back into fashion."
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
New school blockades
Student protesters complained the police did not authorise a march through the centre of the French capital and vowed to stage new blockades of high schools and universities next week.
"Starting this Tuesday, we will blockade our universities and high schools, and we will do so again on Thursday before joining the demonstration on November 5 called by workers and trade unions," said Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for the Student Union.
Ahead of the protests, some shopkeepers barricaded their businesses.
In eastern Paris, Wael Boubaker, a cafe employee, covered a storefront with plywood panels.
"Everyone is staying home. No one is going to come and buy anything," Boubaker said.
Advertisement
Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who accused Macron's government of "taking an increasingly authoritarian turn", joined the march in Paris.
With the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in its debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.
Alain Di Crescenzo, president of France's chamber of commerce, said business owners were worried.
"Shopkeepers can't wait for Saturday to be over," Di Crescenzo told broadcaster France Inter.
Nunez said authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening that urged protesters to spark a "revolution".

articles.title: Inside France: Fake news and avocado sandwiches
articles.text:
Inside France: Fake news and avocado sandwiches
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Fake news and avocado sandwiches
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 31 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 12:10 CET
Add a comment
Protesters including one holding a placard reading "Eggplant, zucchini, avocado, brocoli, even the vegetables are too expensive" referencing leftist slogan ACAB ("All Cops are Bastards"), pictured at a demo in Toulouse, southwestern France on October 24, 2026. Photo by Matthieu RONDEL / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the tsunami of disinformation about violent social unrest in France to calls to change the date of the French presidential election, via protest-themed sandwiches and ridiculous shark films, here's what we have been talking about in France this week.
I felt a moment of empathy with Emmanuel Macron this week (don't tell anyone, I'll never live it down) as he exasperatedly lashed out at "stupid comments" from world leaders about the recent violent protests in France - he didn't name names but the chief culprits for nonsense about immigration and Islam were US president Donald Trump and Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu.
He also warned that it is "not normal" for France to be in such turmoil just six months before a presidential election.
The same point was made by The Local's politics expert John Lichfield, who has spent 25 years observing France: "It's very unusual to have this kind of social unrest so close to an important election.
Advertisement
"Normally protests start about six months after an election when people get fed up with the person they have just elected - it happened that way with Macron and the Gilets Jaunes in 2018, it happened with Sarkozy too.
"To have protests six months before an election is unusual, and therefore it's difficult to predict which way it's going to go, there isn't a template from the past one can follow."
Those outside France may assume that the country is always on fire or rioting about something - but actually there are long periods of calm, which don't make international headlines for obvious reasons.
And while the country slightly nervously prepares for a third Saturday of protests under tight security, some people are starting to look further ahead - there are even calls for the dates of the presidential election to be moved to avoid the traditional protest day of May 1st (the second round is currently scheduled for May 2nd).
Violence may disrupt an election, but so can disinformation, especially when that is coordinated and deliberate.
The country's foreign minister this week revealed that 60 percent of social media posts falsely linking France's October 17th violence to immigration or Islam came from abroad, with accounts in the US, Israel, Iran, Russia and China the most prominent.
And sometimes, disinformation can be fatal - the man arrested for the shooting in Trappes last week told investigators that he had targeted the town because it was a "hotbed of Islamism", according to the prosecutor.
Trappes, in the outer suburbs of Paris, holds the grim distinction of being the subject of a lot of made-up articles about being 'under Sharia law' or a 'no-go zone for non-whites'. Here's the mayor back in 2021 pleading with people to stop spreading fake news about his town.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Talking France
We discuss the latest on the protests and the fallout of the Trappes terror attack in the Talking France podcast - as well as the controversial new highway in south west France, Beaujolais Nouveau Day and how the French celebrate Halloween. I also learned, thanks to my Breton colleague, that Brittany hosts Samhain festivals every year, in a nod to its Celtic roots. Listen here.
Avocado law
I've written before about the tradition of witty and clever placards at protests, but now the boulangeries are apparently getting in on the act too.
The below 'garde à vue' (arrested) sandwich contains avocado and chicken - avocat in French can mean either avocado or lawyer, while les poulets is a slang term for police.
Advertisement
Sharktastic
And this week we learned that quite possibly the worst film ever made is getting a sequel. Sous la Seine (Under Paris) was an absolutely bonkers tale of killer sharks in the Seine that entered the 'so bad it's hilarious' category - and evidently enough people watched it to persuade Netflix to make a sequel.
Sous la Seine 2 is due out next year. The film ended with the whole of Paris under about 20m of water after an insane finale that involved all the bridges somehow getting accidentally blown up, so I'm fascinated to know what the sequel involves. Popcorn at the ready . . .
PS I was worried that the news from France all seems a bit serious at the moment, so I also wrote a list of all the things to look forward to in November.
Thanks for reading and bon weekend !
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.

articles.title: French Expression of the Day: Mauvaise langue
articles.text:
French Expression of the Day: Mauvaise langue
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French Expression of the Day: Mauvaise langue
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 30 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 09:36 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
You'll hope no one ever accuses you of being a "bad tongue" in France.
Why do I need to know mauvaise langue?
Whether you want to call someone out as a mauvaise langue or steer well clear of them, this expression sums up someone you’ll definitely want to keep an eye on.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
Mauvaise langue, roughly pronounced mo-vehz lahng (listen here), literally means 'bad tongue' or ‘bad language’, or ‘wrong language’.
It can be used in this sense for example - les livres sont dans la mauvaise langue (The books are in the wrong language) but you wouldn't use it for 'bad language' in the sense of swearing - gros mots is the most common way to walk about swearwords, or vulgaire to talk more generally about bad language.
But its idiomatic meaning is a bit more subtle.
If the word langue is taken to mean ‘words’ and mauvais to mean ‘nasty’ or even ‘evil’, you won’t be surprised to learn a mauvaise langue is a way to describe gossips and those who say unkind or even slanderous things behind other people’s backs.
It can also be used in a more light-hearted, less accusatory way of describing someone who has badmouthed someone. In this sense, in English you could translate it as a 'mischief-maker' or a 'scandalmonger'.
Advertisement
An old synonym langue serpentine (‘serpent tongue’) gives an even clearer idea of the slippery, slimy nature of a mauvaise langue.
It’s normally used with the verb être, like elle est mauvaise langue (‘she’s a horrible gossip’) or ils sont mauvaises langues (‘they are horrible gossips’), with an s added to the end of mauvaise in the plural.
Use it like this
Sans vouloir être mauvaise langue, je pense qu'il n'est pas à sa place. - Without wanting to sound like a gossip, I think he’s out of place here.
Les mauvaises langues disent qu'il ne fera pas l'affaire. - The gossips are saying that he won’t get the job done.
Arrête d'être aussi mauvaise langue à son sujet, tu vas le regretter. - Stop bad-mouthing him/her so much, you're going to regret it.

articles.title: 'A lot of arguing to be done': What's at stake in the upcoming EU-UK summit?
articles.text:
'A lot of arguing to be done': What's at stake in the upcoming EU-UK summit?
Advertisement
Politics
'A lot of arguing to be done': What's at stake in the upcoming EU-UK summit?
Claudia Delpero, Europe Street - editorial@thelocal.com
Published: 31 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 10:36 CET
Add a comment
British PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out a return to the EU. Photo: HENRY NICHOLLS / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
Leaders of the EU and the UK will meet for a crucial summit in November with a move towards closer cooperation on the table. But how much will be achieved given the differences and disagreements that exist?
The EU and the UK will hold their second summit after Brexit in Brussels on November 20th.
The summit was planned for July but it was delayed after the resignation of UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer. It will now take place in a different political context, with the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, talking about a national debate on the future relationship with the EU, including the possibility to rejoin and restore free movement of people.
Despite the new narrative, “this summit is really about taking forward some negotiations that were launched at EU-UK summit in May 2025, so the agenda is quite modest, and even that is proving quite challenging to get over the line,” Ian Bond, Deputy Director of the Centre for European Reform, a think tank in London and Brussels, told The Local.
Advertisement
“Both the UK and the EU will try to portray the summit as a success, but the reality is there’s still quite a lot of arguing to be done”, he said.
At the European Parliament debate on the summit last week, European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the EU aims to “complete negotiations… as a package” on trade in agricultural products, the linkage of the EU and the UK carbon markets, and the creation of a youth experience scheme. Negotiations are also ongoing on the UK’s participation in the EU’s electricity market, the Commission added.
Food and electricity
Ian Bond says that the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement is “probably the easiest” to achieve. The agreement will remove trade barriers in food and agricultural products as the UK will commit to adopt the EU's rulebook in the sector.
The UK participation in the EU emissions trading scheme and electricity market should also be agreed. “Both sides want energy trading,” Bond says.
“The offshore wind infrastructure in the North Sea could serve both the UK and the EU, and one of the advantages of being in different time zones is that the peak hours are slightly different on the two sides of the Channel, so there is a benefit to both sides in being able to shift generating capacity back and forth to meet those different peak times,” he added.
In exchange for access to its electricity market, the EU however demands a “quite sizable financial contribution” to the cohesion fund, the programme to reduce disparities among EU regions.
Advertisement
Youth mobility
But the most difficult part of the summit agenda concerns the youth mobility scheme. The scheme will give the opportunity to people aged between 18 and 30 to live, work and travel across the Channel without sponsorship requirements for up to three years.
At the European Parliament debate, Thomas Byrne, Minister for Europe of Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Council presidency, said: “The youth experience scheme is at the heart of our aim to rebuild bridges between the young people across the UK and the EU. It is a key priority.”
Disagreement however persists on the annual cap the UK wants to set on the number of young Europeans who could benefit.
Get our essential newsletter for Britons living in and moving to Europe
The EU also demands that EU students pay home fees in UK universities (currently £9,790) and are exempted from the NHS surcharge. Since the end of free movement, EU students have to pay international fees, which are much higher, as well as the visa and a fee to access the public health service.
According to the Financial Times, the UK offered a “discount”, which EU Member States still consider insufficient.
“This is a problem for both the UK government and universities because British universities are heavily reliant on the fact that overseas students pay much more than home students. If tens of thousands EU students pay lower fees, that could create a hole in their budget that the government might have to fill,” Bond explains.
Another major source of disagreement is the request by the British government that young Brits be allowed to move from one country to another like during the time of EU membership. This would allow them to work anywhere, for example in a bar in Ibiza during the summer and at a ski resort in Austria during the winter. EU countries say instead that they should get a work permit for only one Member State without the automatic right to move to another.
“This is not a European Commission competence as it is up to each Member State to decide what they do about work visas,” Bond says.
According to media reports, the agreement on the youth experience scheme might be delayed by six months to ensure a positive outcome of the summit.
Advertisement
‘Made in Europe’ and foreign policy
Another issue in discussion will be whether the UK will be included in the ‘Made in Europe’ provisions the EU is discussing to boost local manufacturing and reduce dependence on countries like China. These provisions will concern public procurement and key sectors such as electric cars, aluminium and steel and clean technologies, for which the EU wants to increase local production.
Foreign policy will also be on the agenda, with conclusions expected on support for Ukraine and defence cooperation.
“Apart from these milestones, work is ongoing on strengthening ties in many other areas of mutual interest. This includes health security, police cooperation, judicial cooperation and tackling irregular migration and smugglers’ networks,” Byrne told the Euro

articles.title: Protests in France: What to expect on October 31st
articles.text:
Protests in France: What to expect on October 31st

Protests

Protests in France: What to expect on October 31st
Emma Albright - emma.albright@thelocal.com
Published: 26 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 09:07 CET
Add a comment
Protesters take part in a demonstration in Paris on October 24th. (Photo by Aris MESSINIS / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
Saturday, October 31st, will be another day of protests in France, with the Interior Minister warning of a high risk of violence - across France, 70,000 police will be deployed. Here's what to expect.
The Gilets Jaunes have called for a third day of protests on Saturday, dubbed “Act III - Halloween”, focusing on public freedoms and the right to demonstrate, while the lycée students will also stage protests and unions have organised marches in some towns.
The Gilets Jaunes organisers are planning sit-ins outside town halls as well as casserolades (noisy protests involving banging saucepans), but unions and student leaders are planning more traditional marches.
Several events have been denied authorisation while there will be a very heavy police presence, with 70,000 officers mobilised across France.
Advertisement
Here is what we know so far about the planned protests;
The Gilets Jaunes had called for gatherings and sit-ins outside préfectures, mairies and the French parliament, rather than marches or demos, along with casserolades (noisy protests involving banging pots and pans).
However, in some towns unions have also organised more traditional demos, which lycée student leaders say they intend to join.
However, local authorities have refused to authorise events in several of the bigger cities, proposing alternative routes that keep demos out of the city centres.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has warned of a 'high risk of violence' and says that 70,000 police will be deployed across the country.
Paris
In Paris, Gilets Jaunes had called for sit-ins and a casserolade outside the Assemblée nationale (French parliament), while unions had proposed a march from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation at 2pm on Saturday.
Police refused to allow either event and have instead proposed a march route at the eastern edge of the city, going from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton. There will also be multiple Metro closures and disruption on the trams.
Find the latest here MAP: Routes and Metro for the Paris protest march on October 31st
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Why are the Gilets Jaunes focusing on public freedoms?
The movement's demands have shifted since October 17th, when protesters focused on the rising cost of living and fuel prices in the country.
For the latest mobilisation, organisers are criticising what they describe as the government's increasingly authoritarian approach, following restrictions on demonstrations and night-time curfews in several cities.
They are calling for curfews to be lifted, an amnesty for protesters who have been arrested and investigations into alleged violence by law enforcement officers.
They also want to bring together school pupils, university students, workers, farmers and retirees in a convergence des luttes - a gathering of different social movements.
Advertisement
Will lycée students join the protests on October 31st?
Lycée students have been another driving force behind the wider mobilisation, with protests spreading across France since mid-September. Early October saw teenagers blockading schools to protest against a lack of resources and demand changes to the education system.
READ ALSO: Analysis: Are French lycées really all that bad?
Lycée student leaders have confirmed that they will join October 31st events, calling on teenagers across France to join events in their local towns and cities after rejecting the government's education reforms as insufficient.
Further blockades at high schools and university campuses are also possible when classes resume on Monday, November 2nd, following the Toussaint school holidays (All Saints' Day).
The next planned day of protest at schools is Tuesday, November 3rd, while students will also join the cross-sector day of strikes on Thursday, November 5th.
Advertisement
Unions call for wider strikes in November
Trade unions are also calling for a n ationwide day of strikes and demonstrations on Thursday, November 5th. Rail workers are being encouraged to join the movement, meaning transport disruption could be more significant.
READ ALSO: French rail workers join November strike
Almost all major unions have called for workers to take part in action over wages, pensions and public services. France's hardline CGT union has also called for strikes to be expanded from November 5th onwards.

articles.text:
MAPS: Routes and Metro closures for the Paris demo on October 31st

Protests
Members only
MAPS: Routes and Metro closures for the Paris demo on October 31st
Emma Albright - emma.albright@thelocal.com
Published: 28 Oct, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 31 Oct 2026 08:57 CET
1 comment
An empty avenue in Paris on October 24th, 2026, on the day of nationwide protests. (Photo by Olivier MORIN / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
As Paris prepares for another demonstration against the rising cost of living, here's a look at the route for approves demos, plus the Metro, tram and RER closures.
Up to 40 Metro stations will be closed, meanwhile the exact route for the demos has involved multiple legal challenges.
The October 31st protests are part of a wider mobilisation against the rising cost of living. The October 17th demonstration degenerated into widespread violence and looting, prompting tighter security measures for subsequent protests.
Two marches had been proposed - the Gilets Jaunes wanted to take a route between Bastille and Concorde, finishing up at the Assemblée nationale.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
Meanwhile, unions had proposed a route starting at Bastille and taking an indirect route to Place de la Nation.
Below is the union's proposed route, which, at the time of writing, is not authorised.
Instead, police proposed a route between Porte de Bagnolet and Porte de Charenton, following the Boulevards des Maréchaux around the eastern edge of the capital - as shown below.
The police have authorised a gathering between 12pm and 6pm between the two destinations, with the march starting at 2pm along the Boulevards des Maréchaux.
Unions appealed against the ban and won, but then the Conseil d'Etat ruled against them - which means that the above route is the only officially authorised one.
This route goes along the tram track, so trams will be halted in the eastern part of the city (full details on all transport closures below).
The decision follows comments by President Emmanuel Macron earlier this week that demonstrations should be kept away from city centres to protect shops and businesses.
Advertisement
The Yellow Vests coordination group has also declared a more central route for October 31st, starting at Place de la Bastille at 2pm and heading towards the National Assembly (Assemblée nationale).
The proposed march would pass through Place de la République, the Grands Boulevards, Place de l'Opéra, Place de la Madeleine and Place de la Concorde.
This route - below - has not been authorised to go ahead.
In an interview with French daily Le Parisien, Paris police chief Patrice Faure said traditional demonstrations between Place de la République, Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation would not be allowed "for some time", arguing that the conditions were not in place to guarantee public safety.
Advertisement
The Yellow Vests coordination group also cancelled a planned gathering outside the National Assembly on Friday evening after police refused to authorise it. The group had planned a 'casserolade' (a demonstration in which participants bang pots and pans) from 6pm to 9pm, as part of its campaign to defend civil liberties.
Metro closures
There is also a lengthy list of planned station closures - this could change throughout the day, so travellers are advised to keep up to date with the latest with a travel app like CityMapper or Google Maps.
Where Metro stations are closed, the trains continue through without stopping. It does not mean that the line is halted.
Closed all day - Argentine, Assemblée nationale, Champs-Élysées-Clémenceau, Étoile, Concorde, Franklin Roosevelt, George V, Invalides, Madeleine, Miromesnil, Rue du Bac, Saint-Augustin, Saint-Philippe-du-Roule, Solférino, Sèvres-Babylone, Tuileries, Vaneau and Varenne.
Closed from 9am - Bastille, Bréguet-Sabin, Chemin Vert, Filles du Calvaire, République, Saint-François-Xavier and Saint-Sébastien-Froissart.
Closed from 11am - Chaussées d’Antin-Lafayette, Opéra, Pyramides.
Closed from 8pm - Access to Châtelet-les-Halles station, which serves multiple Metro lines as well as RER B and C, will be closed from 8pm
Closed from midday - Bel-Air, Cluny-La Sorbonne, Mabillon, Maubert-Mutualité, Michel Bizot, Odéon, Picpus, Porte de Montreuil, Porte Dorée, Saint-Germain-des-Prés.
Taffic halted - traffic will be halted on Line 6 between Charles de Gaulle-Étoile and Kléber, and on line 11 between Chatelet and Hotel de Ville.
Tram - because the authorised demo route follows the tram tracks, traffic will be totally halted on large sections of the tram - line T3a between Porte de Vincennes and Stade Charléty and T3b between Porte de Vincennes and Porte des Lilas.
Curfew - there will also be a limited curfew in place between 11pm and 6am - this concerns only the Place de la République and the area immediately around Châtelet-les-Halles. People who live or work in those areas are exempted.
